title: Unbelievable!
bubbles: Because her husband had left her behind.
sources: SB p.94–95 (PDF 95–96), Grammar Bank p.148–149 (PDF 149–150), Communication p.106/107/112 (PDF 107/108/113); WB p.82–83 (PDF 81–82), key WB p.95 (PDF 94). Scripts 12.1–12.2 are not printed in the SB (answers by the recordings)

reference.title: Glossary
reference.text: RSPCA – Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (a British charity that helps animals).

reference.title: Telling a news story
reference.text: Start with where and when: Last Sunday, in Sydney… Then say what happened (past simple): A police car went to the apartment immediately. Use the past perfect for things that happened earlier: The callers had heard a woman screaming.

tasks.instruction: Read the three news stories. Match them to the headlines
tasks.note: SB 1a+1b: догадки по картинкам (1a) проверяются чтением (1b) → Blank: заголовок к каждой истории; картинки с заголовками — SB p.94. Ответы по тексту (MODEL)
tasks.context:
Story 1. Last Sunday at about 2.00 a.m., police in Sydney, Australia, received several phone calls about shouting and loud noises that were coming from an apartment in a suburb of the city. The callers had heard a woman screaming, a man shouting ‘I’m going to kill you! You’re dead!’, and somebody throwing furniture.
A police car went to the apartment immediately. A man opened the door.
‘Where’s your wife?’ the officer asked.
‘I don’t have one,’ the man replied.
‘Where’s your girlfriend?’
‘I don’t have one,’ the man replied again.
The officer told the man that his neighbours had heard shouting and screaming.
‘Come on, what have you done to her?’ the officer asked.
‘It was a spider,’ the man replied. ‘A really big one.’
‘What about the woman who was screaming?’
‘Yes, sorry, that was me,’ the man said. ‘I really, really hate spiders. I was trying to kill it.’
The police looked around the apartment and confirmed that nobody was hurt. Except the spider.

Story 2. A woman in Worthing, West Sussex, got a big surprise yesterday when she opened a large box of DVDs that she had bought on eBay and a cat suddenly jumped out. The cat, called Cupcake, had got into the box eight days earlier, when her owner Julie Baggott was packing the box to send to her customer. Julie didn’t notice that Cupcake had climbed into the box and fallen asleep.
Julie’s customer called the RSPCA, who collected the cat and took it to a vet. Dr Ben Colwell, who treated Cupcake, said that she was very frightened and very thirsty – the cat had survived the 260-mile journey with no food or water. Luckily Cupcake had a microchip in her neck, so the vet found Julie’s details and phoned her.
Julie had been very sad about losing her cat. She had put up posters and looked for Cupcake for days. ‘I feel terrible,’ said Julie. ‘I put the DVDs in the box and I closed it straight away, so I don’t know how she got in there. It was a miracle she was alive.’

Story 3. An Argentinian family was driving home after a holiday in Brazil when the husband, Walter, made an unfortunate mistake. He stopped at a petrol station, filled up the car with petrol, and went to the toilet. But when he drove off, he didn’t notice that his wife Claudia wasn’t in the car.
Claudia had been asleep in the back seat. While her husband was in the toilet, she woke up and went into the shop to buy some cookies, but when she came back outside she found that her husband had left without her. The couple’s 14-year-old son didn’t notice that his mother wasn’t there because he was playing on his phone in the front seat.
Walter only realized his wife wasn’t in the car after he’d driven 100 kilometres. Meanwhile, Claudia tried to phone him, but she couldn’t get a signal, so she asked the petrol station manager for help. He contacted the local police, who took her to the police station. Her husband eventually returned to pick her up two hours later. When he arrived, Claudia was so angry that all she could do was scream and kick the car.

tasks.context:
Story A. In Sydney, early in the morning, some swimmers were having a swim in an outdoor swimming pool which was very close to the sea. The swimmers were very surprised when suddenly the pool assistant started shouting ‘Get out of the water! Quickly!’ The swimmers immediately got out. Then they realized that there was a shark at the other end! A large wave had carried the shark into the pool overnight. Fortunately none of the swimmers were hurt, and the shark was caught in a net and put back into the sea.

Story B. Last Monday workers in the luggage area at Stockholm’s Arlanda airport, in Sweden, got a big surprise. They were taking suitcases off the luggage belt to put them on the different planes, when suddenly they saw an old lady sitting on the belt next to her suitcase. The woman had got confused at the check-in desk. She had put her luggage on the belt and then had sat down on the belt herself. A spokesman at the airport said ‘Unfortunately, she did not understand when she was given check-in instructions. She got on the belt together with her bag. Luckily, it wasn’t a long ride – only a few metres.’

exercises.situation: Speaking practice in an English class (level: pre-intermediate) after reading unusual news stories. The student is Student A and tells you a story from memory: in Sydney, early in the morning, some swimmers were in an outdoor pool close to the sea; suddenly the pool assistant shouted ‘Get out of the water! Quickly!’; they got out and saw a shark at the other end; a large wave had carried the shark into the pool in the night; nobody was hurt, and the shark was caught in a net and put back into the sea. Listen, react (Really? That’s unbelievable!) and ask one or two questions (What had happened in the night? Was anybody hurt?). Then you are Student B: tell your story in 4–5 short sentences: last Monday workers in the luggage area at Stockholm’s Arlanda airport saw an old lady sitting on the luggage belt next to her suitcase; she had got confused at the check-in desk; she had put her luggage on the belt and then had sat down on it herself; luckily it was only a few metres. Finally ask which of the stories in the lesson (the spider in Sydney, the cat in the box of DVDs, the wife left at the petrol station, the shark, the old lady) they find the most unbelievable, and if there have been any funny or unusual stories in the news recently. If the student makes a mistake with the past perfect or the past simple, repeat the correct form naturally in your reply.
exercises.goal: Tell the shark story, listen to the airport story, and say which story is the most unbelievable.
exercises.opener: Hi! I hear you read a crazy news story. Go on, tell me – what happened?
criteria: tells the shark story in a logical order (where, what the assistant shouted, the shark, what had happened in the night, the end)
uses the past perfect at least once correctly (A wave had carried the shark into the pool)
uses at least two time expressions (suddenly, immediately, straight away, meanwhile, eventually)
reacts to the airport story and says which story they find the most unbelievable and why

steps.text: Say where and when it happened
steps.example: This happened at a swimming pool in Sydney, early in the morning.
Suddenly the pool assistant shouted ‘Get out of the water!’ and the swimmers got out immediately.

steps.text: Explain what had happened in the night
steps.example: There was a shark in the pool. A big wave had carried it in during the night.
Nobody was hurt, and they put the shark back into the sea.

steps.text: Listen to the airport story and choose the most unbelievable story
steps.example: I think the story about the cat is the most unbelievable. It had travelled 260 miles in a box!

reference.title: Time expressions
rows: A police car went to the apartment immediately.
I put the DVDs in the box and I closed it straight away.
Meanwhile, Claudia tried to phone him.
Her husband eventually returned two hours later.

reference.title: Position
reference.text: suddenly, meanwhile and eventually often go at the beginning of a sentence (Suddenly, the lights went off.) or before the main verb (He eventually arrived.). immediately and straight away usually go at the end: Get up immediately! I’ll do it straight away.

reference.wrong: Eventually means ‘maybe, possibly’: I’ll eventually come to the party.
reference.right: Eventually means ‘in the end, after a long time’: After two hours, he eventually arrived.
reference.why: eventually is a false friend – it does not mean ‘possibly’.

reference.title: Past perfect
rows: When I woke up the garden was all white. It had snowed during the night. I suddenly realized that I’d left my phone in the taxi.
We got home just in time – the match hadn’t started. When she got to class, she realized that she hadn’t brought her book.
A: I went to Paris last weekend. I really loved it. B: Had you been there before? A: No, I hadn’t.

reference.text: We use the past perfect when we are already talking about the past and want to talk about an earlier past action: When I woke up the garden was all white. It had snowed during the night. (= It snowed before I woke up.)

reference.title: Form
reference.text: had / hadn’t + past participle. The form is the same for all persons: I / you / he / she / we / they had left. Contraction: ’d (I’d left, she’d gone).

reference.title: had or would?
reference.text: ’d can be had or would. I didn’t know that you’d found a new job. (’d = had + past participle) If you went by taxi, you’d get there much quicker. (’d = would + infinitive)

reference.wrong: When we arrived, the film already started.
reference.right: When we arrived, the film had already started.
reference.why: The film started before we arrived – an earlier past action needs the past perfect.

questions.text: Where were you going, and when?
questions.hint: (This happened when I was going to…)
(Eventually I got to…, but it had already left.)

criteria: says where and when it happened
uses the past perfect at least once (the train had already left)
uses at least one time expression (suddenly, immediately, eventually, meanwhile)

exercises.prompt: Write about a time you tried to meet a friend and something went wrong. Example: A few weeks ago, I arranged to meet my friend Jack at the football stadium. I arrived at 6.30, but he wasn’t there. He was at home watching TV because he’d forgotten. Eventually I went in and watched the match, but I was really angry with him.

questions.text: Who were you going to meet, and where?

questions.hint: (I arrived at…, but she wasn’t there.)

questions.text: What was your friend doing, or what had they done?

criteria: says who they were meeting and where
uses the past perfect at least once (he’d forgotten)

tasks.instruction: Complete the sentences with the past perfect of the verbs in brackets.

exercises.text: When I got to the party, everybody {}.
exercises.explain: They went home before I arrived: had + gone.

exercises.text: I couldn’t pay for lunch because I {} my wallet at home.
exercises.explain: Leaving the wallet was earlier: had left.

exercises.text: She was very tired because she {} all night.
exercises.explain: Negative past perfect: hadn’t + past participle (sleep – slept – slept).

exercises.text: The kitchen was a mess because the children {} a cake.
exercises.explain: make – made – made: had made.

exercises.text: {} you ever {} sushi before you went to Japan?
exercises.explain: Question: Had + subject + past participle.

exercises.text: We didn’t recognize the town because it {} so much.
exercises.explain: The town changed before we saw it again.

exercises.text: He failed the exam because he {} enough.
exercises.explain: Negative: hadn’t studied.

exercises.text: When the police arrived, the thieves {}.
exercises.explain: The thieves escaped first: had escaped.

tasks.instruction: Complete the sentences with the past simple or the past perfect of the verbs in brackets.

exercises.text: When I {} home, my brother {} all the pizza.
exercises.explain: My brother ate the pizza first (past perfect); then I got home (past simple).

exercises.text: I {} the film because I {} the book.
exercises.explain: Reading the book happened earlier: had already read.

exercises.text: She {} that she {} her keys in the office.
exercises.explain: realized (past simple) + what happened before (past perfect).

exercises.text: By the time we {} at the station, the train {}.
exercises.explain: by the time + past simple; the earlier action: past perfect.

exercises.text: It was the first time I {} on a plane, so I {} very nervous.
exercises.explain: It was the first time + past perfect.

exercises.text: He {} me the photos he {} on holiday.
exercises.explain: He took the photos before he showed them.

tasks.instruction: Correct the mistakes. If a sentence is correct, leave it as it is.

exercises.prompt: When we got to the cinema, the film already started.
answers: When we got to the cinema, the film had already started.
When we got to the cinema the film had already started.
exercises.explain: The film started before we got there: had already started.

exercises.prompt: I didn’t know that she had went to Paris.
answers: I didn’t know that she had gone to Paris.
I did not know that she had gone to Paris.
I didn’t know that she’d gone to Paris.
exercises.explain: had + past participle: gone, not went.

exercises.prompt: They were hungry because they hadn’t eaten all day.
answers: They were hungry because they hadn’t eaten all day.
exercises.explain: Correct: hadn’t + past participle.

exercises.prompt: Did you had been there before?
answers: Had you been there before?
exercises.explain: Past perfect question: Had + you + been (no did).

exercises.prompt: She has forgotten her umbrella, so she got wet.
answers: She had forgotten her umbrella, so she got wet.
She’d forgotten her umbrella, so she got wet.
She forgot her umbrella, so she got wet.
exercises.explain: We are talking about the past, so the earlier action is had forgotten, not has forgotten.

exercises.prompt: When I arrived, Tom had just left.
answers: When I arrived, Tom had just left.
exercises.explain: Correct: had just left = he left a moment before I arrived.

reference.title: The letter i
reference.text: The letter i is usually pronounced /aɪ/ before a consonant + e, e.g. drive, and is pronounced /ɪ/ between two consonants if there is no e, e.g. mistake. Some common words don’t follow the rules: driven and notice have an e, but i is /ɪ/.
